prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength serve as a Doppler- and recoil-free frequency reference, and for its development to a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B040 as a stand-alone prize to Katori and Ye. The one-sentence answer to the chair's first question is this. A frequency comb counts optical cycles, and a trapped ion is one isolated quantum system, whereas the lattice clock interrogates a very large number of neutral atoms at once, each held in its own lattice site, with the trap light shift cancelled by choosing the magic wavelength, so that the atoms are free of Doppler and recoil shifts and the statistical power of an ensemble is combined with the cleanliness of a single ion. That is a new experimental regime and not a refinement of the earlier ones. It is also physics and not only instrumentation, since the same system has delivered millimetre-scale tests of the gravitational redshift, new bounds on variation of constants and dark-matter searches, and has led to many-body clocks with Fermi-degenerate gases. Reproduction is the point I weigh most: several national laboratories have compared lattice clocks at the 10^-18 level, which is exactly the independent confirmation I look for. The two names split by contribution type, Katori for the magic-wavelength concept and first lattice clock, Ye for the record accuracy and the many-body regime, and that is a clean split.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is a real argument, and I would not call it empty, but I now think it is answered by the distinction between a ruler, a single-ion device and a many-atom lattice. The remaining weaknesses are these. The redefinition of the second has not been adopted, so the largest application is prospective, although I regard the physics as already verified and the redefinition as a procedural matter for the metrology bodies. The attribution to two names rests on my reading of the Tokyo and JILA histories, and I have not been able to verify priority details independently. Lemonde, Gill, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom and Takamoto all did important work, and a critic could argue that a third name is justified. I am also close to this community, so my own ranking should be discounted accordingly.

responses.point: Kroll's round-1 split of the credit by contribution type, Katori for the magic-wavelength proposal and first strontium lattice clock, Ye for accuracy, stability and the many-body clock, and his view that the multi-atom Doppler- and recoil-free interrogation is not contained in the comb or in ion clocks.
responses.response: We agree, and the chair asked the two of us for wording. My draft is: for the invention of the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength serve as a Doppler- and recoil-free frequency reference, and for its development to a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18. The first half is Katori's and the second half is Ye's, and the citation says so without a ranking. I would add that I have moved on B017 as you have: Chu's absence and the 1991 near-simultaneous demonstrations make a three-name allocation harder to defend than I allowed in round 1. I therefore keep B017 only as a second alternative.

responses.point: Danielsson wants the external expert reports to address Lemonde, Gill and others before the committee commits to two names, and he also pairs B040 with B028 (Hosono) as a two-part prize.
responses.response: I share the wish to settle the credit question, and I would not defend a third name unless the experts show a contribution of the same weight as the other two. My reading is that Lemonde, Gill, Ludlow, Hinkley and Bloom made decisive contributions to the clocks and to systematic evaluation, but the scheme and the first lattice clocks, and the accuracy and many-body regime, are the two clearly separable achievements. A citation that names the invention and the development does not take priority away from anyone. On the pairing with Hosono, I respect the discovery, but I do not support it. A prize with no common thread is a compromise, and I would not add a second part to a mature, clean two-name case merely to fill the third seat. If nothing else is as well attributed, a single part is the better prize.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B061 as a stand-alone prize but calls B040 the better-attributed fallback, and in round 1 ranked B040 fifth because of the overlap with 2005 and 2012 and the pending redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I take the concern about a third award for better clocks seriously, and I hope the answer above addresses it: the lattice clock changes what is being measured, an ensemble of independent atoms, and not only how well. The 2022 prize was about entanglement and Bell tests, so I do not see a recent AMO prize that duplicates it. Your fallback is welcome, since it means the committee has two attributable candidates and not one. On B061 I still think the physics is the larger conceptual shift, and I would be comfortable with it in a later year, but with Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang outside the names I cannot prefer it now, and your own round-1 reply describes the HgTe step as the reason Molenkamp's group knew what to grow.

responses.point: Eriksson holds that the BHZ gap in B061 can be handled by citation wording around the prediction and observation of the quantum spin Hall effect, and that the 2016 prize covered phase transitions and not time-reversal-invariant topological insulators.
responses.response: That is a reasonable position and I defer to you on condensed matter. I accept the 2016 distinction: a Z2 class with helical edge states is not the same thing as the integer quantum Hall topology of Thouless and Haldane. My difficulty is only with the credit. A citation can name the prediction and its first observation, but the HgTe proposal is the link between them, and a reader will ask why it was set aside. You say it is your strongest reservation, and I agree with that ranking of the reservations. I therefore keep B061 as my first alternative, and I would move to it if the committee found B040 cannot be allocated to two names, but I do not move it above B040. I also thank you for the explanation of why B040 is a physics discovery, which I accept as the right test.

responses.point: Olsson pairs B040 with B028 (Hosono) because both parts are mature and cleanly credited, and she regards the pairing mechanism of the iron-based superconductors as no reason to wait.
responses.response: I agree that B028 is a mature discovery that has stood for eighteen years and is unusually cleanly credited, and I agree that the mechanism is no reason to wait. My objection is different. I am an atomic theorist and cannot judge the early Tc increases by the Chinese groups, so I defer to you and Danielsson on that. What I can judge is that the two parts have no shared idea, and that adding a second part changes a prize whose logic is clear into one whose logic is a matter of balance. I would support B028 if the committee wanted a second part, but I would not argue for it myself, and I did not list it among my alternatives for that reason.

uncertainties: Priority between the Tokyo and JILA efforts and the weight of Lemonde, Gill, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom and Takamoto remain unverified by me, and I rely on the external expert reports for this.
Whether the committee reads the pending redefinition of the second as confirmation or as evidence that the case is prospective.
Whether the HgTe credit gap in B061 could be repaired by citation wording, which would change my first alternative into a real competitor.
I have not seen any new evidence since round 1, and my change in position is limited to deprioritising B017.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. I have no documented collaboration with Katori or Ye. I am a theoretical atomic physicist in the same broad AMO precision-measurement community, and a long-time collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate, not a candidate here). Kroll's disclosed ties to the Hall laboratory and Johansson's WACQT role do not affect my judgement of B040. I accept scrutiny of my ranking of B040 for this reason, and I am willing to defer to the committee if it judges that my closeness to the field outweighs my view.
